title: A homeowner's credit record can raise the price of disaster protection alongside physical risk
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 34848; approximately 70 million mortgage-linked insurance policies matched to property-level disaster risk and a Washington State natural experiment
geography: United States homeowners insurance and mortgage-linked policies; credit-pricing natural experiment in Washington State

observations.period: Insurance and mortgage-linked records with 2026 paper; Washington credit-information policy change

credit_premium.value: homeowners with low credit scores paid about 24% more for identical coverage than high-credit-score homeowners

risk_comparison.value: credit scores affected insurance premiums about as much as disaster risk in the study

policy_natural_experiment.value: banning credit information in Washington substantially weakened the relationship between credit score and insurance pricing

housing_affordability.value: the authors identify insurance as an often-overlooked component of home affordability, with low credit raising premiums roughly as much as it raises mortgage rates

observations.method: The authors link mortgage-associated insurance policies to property-level disaster risk and use a natural experiment from Washington State's restriction on credit information in insurance pricing to study the credit-score premium relationship.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not follow each owner through renewal, escrow, coverage reduction, nonrenewal, repair, sale, move, claim, or food and care tradeoffs. The 24% estimate concerns identical coverage in the study and does not establish a universal premium or a particular household's affordability threshold.
observations.subgroup: Homeowners with mortgage-linked insurance policies, separated by credit score and property-level disaster risk; income, liquidity, lender requirements, insurer availability, deductible, coverage exclusions, and state rules can differ substantially.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit information may correlate with unobserved risk or insurer costs, and restricting its use can change pricing without guaranteeing lower total housing risk. A higher premium may preserve protection, while a lower premium may have a larger deductible or exclusions. A premium increase does not itself prove a forced move or uninsured loss.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 34848
Related NBER property-insurance study supplies a separate disaster-risk-to-premium comparison using mortgage escrow data

boundary: This record adds a protection-price pathway: credit and physical risk can both enter the cost of keeping a home insured. It does not establish a same-owner path from premium to escrow trouble, coverage cut, repair, sale, move, claim recovery, or complete housing security.
